In Lesson 23 they planned and began drafting a modern retelling of a myth; today they complete it.","enduringUnderstanding":"Stories from different times and cultures share patterns, such as heroes, warnings and transformations, but each storyteller can reshape setting and details to say something new.","futureLessons":"In Lesson 25, students return to the novel with Chapter 18 and analyze how the Underworld entrance is set up, applying the same attention to setting and detail that they used as writers today.","performanceTask":"In Shared Stories, Shared Lessons, students must revise a narrative so it clearly shows how it reinterprets a myth. Today's explanation of what was kept and what was changed practices that skill."},"vocabulary":[{"word":"archetype","definition":"a pattern, character type or situation that appears again and again in stories across cultures","tier":"addressed"},{"word":"retelling","definition":"a new version of an existing story that keeps some of its key parts","tier":"addressed"},{"word":"reinterpret","definition":"to understand or present something in a new way","tier":"addressed"},{"word":"revise","definition":"to change writing to make the ideas, organization or details stronger","tier":"support"},{"word":"adverbial","definition":"a word or phrase that tells when, where, how or why something happens","tier":"support"}],"texts":[{"title":"The Lightning Thief","author":"Rick Riordan","pages":"Chapter 18, pp. 283–top of 291 (homework)"}]},"sections":[{"kind":"launch","title":"Launch","purpose":"Reconnect students with their drafts and the idea that a story can keep a pattern while changing its details.","activities":[{"id":"launch-turn-and-talk","title":"Same Pattern, New Story","minutes":5,"standards":["RL.6.9"],"routine":"Turn and Talk","blocks":[{"type":"directions","text":"Take out your draft and your plan from Lesson 23. Tell a partner: Which myth or archetype (hero, cautionary or transformation) is your story built on, and what is one thing you changed about it?"},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"Think about Percy's quest in The Lightning Thief. It echoes old hero myths, but it takes place in modern New York. What stays the same, and what changes?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"The pattern stays the same: a young hero gets a call, goes on a dangerous journey, and is tested. But Percy rides a bus and a train instead of sailing a ship, and he has ADHD and dyslexia, which the old heroes never did."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"Today you finish your own story and then explain what you kept from the original and what you changed. That explanation shows how your story sends its own message."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"tip","text":"Keep this to 5 minutes. Circulate and listen for students who cannot yet name their archetype. Remind them to check their Lesson 23 plan."}]}]},{"kind":"literacy-lab","title":"Literacy Lab","purpose":"Teach compare/classify sentence frames and adverbials so students can explain how their retelling honors an original myth while changing it.","activities":[{"id":"lab-compare-frames","title":"Language Study: Comparing a Myth and a Retelling","minutes":10,"standards":["RL.6.9","W.6.4","L.6.3"],"routine":"Language Study","blocks":[{"type":"teacher-script","move":"teach","text":"When we compare two versions of a story, we name what is the same and what is different. Writers use frames such as \"In the original myth..., but in my story...\" and \"Both versions show..., however my version...\" to make that comparison clear."},{"type":"paragraph","audience":"teacher","text":"Model with a sample retelling. Write on the board: Original myth: Arachne boasts that she weaves better than the goddess Athena and is turned into a spider. Retelling: Mia posts online that she is the best digital artist in school and loses her account and her friends' trust."},{"type":"directions","text":"Read the model sentences with your teacher. Then identify what is kept (character role, plot pattern, message) and what is changed (setting, details)."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"Model sentence: In the original myth, Arachne weaves in ancient Greece and is turned into a spider, but in my story, Mia posts her art online and loses her account. Both versions show that pride can lead to a downfall; however, my version suggests that bragging in public can cost you real friendships."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"Which parts did the writer keep, and which did the writer change?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"She kept the proud character, the plot where pride leads to punishment, and the message about pride. She changed the setting from Greece to online, and the punishment from a spider to losing her account."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"Look at the phrases \"in ancient Greece\" and \"in public.\" What do they add, and how do they help the reader?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"They tell where and how things happen. They add detail so the reader can picture the setting and understand the difference."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"teach","text":"Those are adverbials: words and phrases that tell when, where, how or why. Use them to add precise detail to your story and to your comparison sentences."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"note","text":"Post the two frames where students can see them. Students will use them in Learning in Action Part B."},{"type":"eld-panel","purpose":"Help students use comparison language and add details with adverbials.","sayAsk":"Say: Let's compare out loud. In the original myth, ___, but in my story, ___. Both versions show ___; however, my version ___. Ask: Where does it happen? When? How? Add an adverbial: quietly, in the school hallway, after the game. Model: You said she lost her friends; we can say she slowly lost her friends after the post went viral.","watchFor":"If students list differences without naming what stayed the same, then ask: What pattern or message is still in both stories? If students use only simple adverbs, then offer a place or time phrase to add. Success: the student completes both frames orally and adds at least one adverbial."},{"type":"support-table","rows":[{"situation":"Struggling with: naming what was kept versus changed","tryThis":"Give a two-column organizer, Kept / Changed, with the rows character roles, plot pattern, central message, setting, details. Complete one row together."},{"situation":"Ready for extension","tryThis":"Ask students to add a third frame, such as \"Although both stories..., my version emphasizes...\", and to explain why their changed setting shifts the message."}]}]}]},{"kind":"learning-in-action","title":"Learning in Action","purpose":"Part A: students finish and revise their archetype-based story (W.6.3, W.6.4). Part B: students explain how the retelling honors the original and changes details (RL.6.9) and give peer feedback in a formative checkpoint.","activities":[{"id":"lia-finish-revise-story","title":"Part A: Finish and Revise the Story","minutes":15,"standards":["W.6.3","W.6.4"],"routine":"Quick Write","blocks":[{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"Writers do not stop at the last sentence. They finish the story, then reread and revise to make sure the setting, details and ending work. Let's look at what a strong narrative needs."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"teach","text":"Think aloud: My story is about a girl who brags online. My ending says, 'She learned her lesson.' That is flat. I will revise to show it: 'Mia deleted the post slowly and typed an apology, hoping it was not too late.' Now the ending follows from the events and shows the change."},{"type":"directions","text":"Finish your draft. Then revise using this checklist: (1) the opening introduces the setting and characters; (2) events happen in a logical order with transitions such as after, meanwhile, by morning; (3) dialogue, pacing or description develops a character or event; (4) precise words and sensory details; (5) a conclusion that follows from the events; (6) a clear archetype (hero, cautionary or transformation). Edit for capitalization, punctuation and spelling."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What is one revision you will make to show your archetype's pattern more clearly?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"My story is a transformation. I need to show more of the middle, where my character slowly starts to change, so I will add a scene with dialogue where he shows he is changing."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"tip","text":"Confer first with students who have not reached an ending. Encourage them to write a short ending rather than a perfect one. Remind students who finished early to revise, not just reread."},{"type":"pulse-check","standards":["W.6.3"],"stem":"A student's draft ends with: \"She learned her lesson and everyone was happy.\" Which revision best follows W.6.3.e by making the conclusion follow from the events?","choices":[{"text":"The end. I hope you liked my story.","correct":false,"rationale":"This is a closing remark to the reader, not a conclusion that follows from the narrated events."},{"text":"After taking down the post, Mia walked into school and apologized to her friends; some forgave her, and she was careful about how she shared her work from then on.","correct":true,"rationale":"It continues the events, shows the character's change and connects directly to the story's message."},{"text":"Mia was very good at art and had many followers online.","correct":false,"rationale":"This repeats an early detail instead of resolving the events."},{"text":"Suddenly a dragon appeared and carried her away.","correct":false,"rationale":"This introduces a new, unrelated event, so the ending does not follow from the story."}]},{"type":"eld-panel","purpose":"Support students in finishing narrative writing with precise details and transitions, and in expanding sentences with adverbials (ELD.PI.6.10, ELD.PII.6.5).","sayAsk":"Say: Tell your partner your ending first, then write it. Ask: What happens last? How does the character change? Sentence frames: After ___, the character ___. By the end, ___ had learned ___. Model: You said he was sad; we can say he walked slowly down the empty hallway, staring at the floor.","watchFor":"If students write a summary instead of a scene, then prompt: Show me what the character says or does. If students use only 'then,' then offer: after that, meanwhile, by morning. Success: the student writes an ending with a transition and at least one adverbial of time, place or manner."},{"type":"support-table","rows":[{"situation":"Struggling with: finishing the draft","tryThis":"Offer an ending frame: At first, ___. After ___, ___. In the end, ___. Have the student rehearse each sentence orally before writing it."},{"situation":"Ready for extension","tryThis":"Ask students to revise the opening or a key moment to add dialogue, a shift in pacing, or a change of point of view that makes the retelling feel distinct."}]}]},{"id":"lia-compare-explain-peer","title":"Part B: Explain the Retelling and Give Peer Feedback","minutes":15,"standards":["RL.6.9","W.6.4","W.6.3"],"routine":"Quick Write and Peer Feedback (Formative Checkpoint)","blocks":[{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"Now explain how your story relates to the original. A strong explanation names what you kept and what you changed, and shows how the change sends a different message."},{"type":"directions","text":"Write 4 to 5 sentences at the end of your story or on a separate page. Use at least one comparison frame: \"In the original myth..., but in my story...\" and \"Both versions show..., however my version...\" Name at least one element you kept (character role, plot pattern or central message) and at least one you changed (setting, details or point of view)."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What message does your changed setting or detail let your story send?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"In the original myth, Arachne is turned into a spider, but in my story, Mia loses her online account. Both versions show that pride can lead to a downfall; however, my version shows that bragging in public can hurt real friendships, not just reputation."},{"type":"directions","text":"Formative Checkpoint: Trade stories with your partner. Read once for meaning. Then give feedback: (1) one thing the story does well (a strong detail, dialogue or ending); (2) one place where the archetype pattern could be clearer; (3) one question about the explanation. Use the frames: I noticed ___. I wonder ___. You could ___. Revise your own piece using your partner's feedback."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"note","text":"Use the checkpoint to see who can name the archetypal pattern and who still lists only differences. Pull those students for a quick conference. Tell pairs that feedback must be specific and kind."},{"type":"eld-panel","purpose":"Support students in comparing the myth and retelling and in evaluating language choices when giving feedback (ELD.PI.6.7).","sayAsk":"Say: Show your partner the words you chose. Ask: Which word or detail makes the setting clear? Frames: One strong word choice is ___ because ___. The setting detail ___ helps me picture ___. In the original ___, but in the retelling ___.","watchFor":"If students say only 'I like it,' then prompt: Which word or detail did you like, and why? If students cannot name what was kept, then prompt: What is the same pattern in both stories? Success: the student names a specific word or detail and explains how it helps the story or its message."},{"type":"support-table","rows":[{"situation":"Struggling with: writing the comparison","tryThis":"Provide the completed frame with blanks and a word bank (hero, pride, journey, setting, message). Have the student say each sentence to a partner first."},{"situation":"Ready for extension","tryThis":"Ask students to add a sentence explaining how a different setting or point of view could have changed the message again, and to revise their story with one new detail that makes the message clearer."}]}]}]},{"kind":"look-back","title":"Look Back","purpose":"Students reflect on how a retelling can keep a pattern and change a message.","activities":[{"id":"lookback-turn-and-talk","title":"Reflect: Keep, Change, Message","minutes":5,"standards":["RL.6.9"],"routine":"Turn and Talk","blocks":[{"type":"directions","text":"Tell your partner what your retelling kept from the original, what it changed, and how the change shapes the message. In the Performance Task you will do this again, so notice what makes your explanation clear."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"How does changing the setting and details let a story keep the same pattern but send a different message?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"The pattern, like a hero's quest or a warning about pride, stays the same, so readers recognize it. But a new setting and new details show how that lesson fits today, so the message is different. Mine says bragging online can hurt real friendships."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"tip","text":"Preview the homework: in Chapter 18, students will see how Riordan describes a modern version of the Underworld entrance."}]}]},{"kind":"homework","title":"Homework (optional)","purpose":"Prepare for Lesson 25 by reading the next section of the novel.","activities":[{"id":"homework-read-ch18","title":"Read and Annotate Chapter 18","minutes":0,"standards":["RL.6.9"],"routine":"Annotation","blocks":[{"type":"text-reference","title":"The Lightning Thief, Chapter 18","pages":"pp. 283–top of 291 (to \"We followed the spirits up a well-worn path.\")"},{"type":"directions","text":"Read Chapter 18 and annotate the text. Mark details about the setting, such as the entrance to the Underworld, that seem modern or that echo the old myths."}]}]}]},"digest":{"summary":"Students finish and revise their archetype-based modern myth retelling, then use compare/classify frames to explain which archetypal elements they kept and which details they changed to send a different message.
